China’s industry ministry and six other agencies set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries, though CATL’s chairman rates the technology four out of nine and calls million-vehicle use before 2030 very unlikely. ProLogium’s Dunkirk plant, the largest new European cell project since Northvolt went bankrupt, is staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and will be certified against a Chinese standard.

China has set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of solid-state batteries. Its biggest battery maker rates the technology four out of nine. A plant in northern France broke ground in February.

The plan came from the industry ministry and six other agencies on 28 September and covers 2026 to 2030, as [CnEVPost reported](https://cnevpost.com/2026/09/28/china-unveils-5-year-battery-plan/). It also targets lithium cells good for 15,000 charge cycles. The ministry acknowledged weaknesses in innovation and imbalances between supply and demand.

CATL is promising less than the plan does. Its chairman, Robin Zeng, put all-solid-state at four out of nine in June, on a scale where nine means ready for vehicle production.

He called the chance of fitting it to a million cars before 2030 very small. CATL intends limited production in 2027.

LG Energy Solution expects the technology to reach smartphones [a decade before EVs](https://thenextweb.com/news/lges-solid-state-batteries-large-format-problem). Its North America president says large cells are where manufacturers struggle.

Europe is further along than that timetable suggests, though not by much, and not on its own technology.

ProLogium already makes [6,000 packs a year](https://thenextweb.com/news/prologium-solid-state-dunkirk-scale) in Taiwan, which is half a gigawatt hour, at 381 Wh/kg on TUV Rheinland’s measurement. That is roughly 30% above the cells in most electric cars today.

The company is now building the same thing in France, with subsidies agreed in 2023 and permits granted the year after.

The Dunkirk plant started construction in February beside the Gravelines nuclear station, staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and 12 GWh by 2032\. Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Mercedes are separately [working with Factorial](https://thenextweb.com/news/factorial-solid-state-coalition-europe) on cells of their own.

None of it is close to Chinese volume, and the gap is not narrowing.

Chinese and South Korean makers supply [90% of Europe’s batteries](https://thenextweb.com/news/after-northvolt-europe-eyes-new-battery-frontiers-beyond-china), and Northvolt went bankrupt after raising $15bn. Dunkirk is the largest new European cell project since.

The standard is Chinese as well. ProLogium’s cells are certified against GB/T 43568-2026, the all-solid-state specification Beijing introduced in July, and were separately tested by UL Solutions.

China took 70% of global electric car production under the previous five-year plan. The new one says initial large-scale use rather than mass production, and even that is a target rather than a promise.

You've shared two recent articles on solid-state batteries — one from **MIT Technology Review** (October 21, 2026) and one from **TopSpeed** about Honda's progress. Here's a synthesized overview of the key points and cross-references between them:

---

## The Promise

Both articles agree on the core value proposition: solid-state batteries (SSBs) replace flammable liquid electrolytes with solid ceramics, sulfides, or polymers, promising **faster charging, longer life, higher energy density, and improved safety** (no thermal runaway fires).

## The Sticking Points

Both sources acknowledge this technology has been "years away" for over a decade:

* **Dendrites:** Needle-like lithium crystals grow during charging and punch through the solid electrolyte. MIT TR notes they crack ceramics like roots in concrete. TopSpeed explains Honda's solution is a thin polymer sheet that prevents lithium from contacting electrodes where dendrites take root — not permanent, but adds "meaningful years" to service life.
* **Manufacturing at scale:** Requires defect-free ceramic sheets and dry rooms (electrolytes react with water). MIT TR says most expect cost parity with Li-ion packs in the **mid-2030s**. TopSpeed's source notes: "it will probably at least take until 2035 before it hits mainstream."

## Where Everyone Stands

| Company | Status |
|---------|--------|
| **Honda** | Opened a *demonstration line* in Sakura, Japan (Jan 2025); claims to be the first automaker with SSB production running. Roll-pressing technique + polymer dendrite barrier. $287M investment. Not full-scale manufacturing yet. |
| **Toyota** | Research since 2010; partnering with Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant. Claims 745-mile range after <10 min charge (if it works). Progress described as "maddeningly slow." |
| **QuantumScape** (Bill Gates-backed) | Announced proprietary large-scale manufacturing method for ceramic electrolytes in 2025. Shortened heat-treatment from days to minutes. Still not in production vehicles. |
| **CATL** (~40% global battery market) | Pumped ~$2.6B into SSB R&D in 2024 alone. Chairman Robin Zeng rates all-solid-state at **4/9 on readiness** and calls fitting it to a million cars before 2030 "very small." Plans limited production in 2027. |
| **BYD** | Yangwang brand testing ultra-luxury sedan with SSBs (flagship model expected ~$300K). Semi-solid already deployed; all-solid-state targeted for limited batches in 2027, scaling to 2030. |
| **China (government)** | Set a national target of first large-scale SSB use by 2030 — but this is described as "a target rather than a promise," not production. |

## The Skeptics' View

The Next Web reporting adds a crucial reality check: **CATL rates the technology at only 4/9 for vehicle production readiness**, and **LG Energy Solution expects SSBs to reach smartphones a decade before EVs** because large-format cells are much harder than small ones. VW's Canadian plant slipped to 2029; Northvolt went bankrupt after raising $15B. Europe now relies on Chinese and Korean suppliers for 90% of its batteries.

## Key Technical Innovation (from Honda)

Honda's main claimed advance is **roll-pressing**: stamping SSB cells together during assembly to "squash out" air pockets in the powder electrolyte, improving electrode contact and density — something liquid/paste electrolytes do naturally by conforming to their container. Plus the thin polymer dendrite barrier. Both are incremental but non-trivial engineering solutions.

---

**Bottom line both articles tell:** The science works in the lab, the capital is flowing, and demand isn't far behind. But the manufacturing gap between a demonstration line and mass production remains enormous, and industry leaders (CATL's chairman being the most prominent skeptic) are keeping expectations grounded. **2030 is a government target, not a delivery.** The likely timeline: ultra-luxury vehicles first (~2027–2030), then costlier mainstream cars in the early 2030s, with widespread adoption arguably post-2035.

Would you like me to dig into any particular aspect — materials science (oxide vs sulfide vs polymer electrolytes), the economics of manufacturing at scale, competitive positioning of specific companies, or something else?
